title: Update 11/13
body: What post-training does to the Assistant and to the roles a model can play, told from the field to my results.
Two model families: OLMo-2-7B (my runs) and Olmo 3 7B (Han Xiao's released data). Every number says which.
Agent checks only. No human has reviewed these analyses yet.

title: Persona research rests on a few foundations, and the newest work asks about training stages
body: A popular view of chat models, the Persona Selection Model, says that pretraining teaches a model many characters and post-training selects one of them, the Assistant.

title: Where the Assistant sits among the roles matters for safety
body: Misalignment can act like a switch to a different persona, and keeping a model near the Assistant on the axis keeps it helpful and resists persona-based jailbreaks.

title: No paper we read shows at which training stage the Assistant becomes special
body: No paper we read shows this with base models included and a check that the words alone do not explain it.

title: I ask at which OLMo-2-7B stage the Assistant becomes privileged
body: Privileged means the default sits at one end of the role map, or its replies vary less than a typical role's replies.
The answer would show where in training the Assistant gets selected, which the Persona Selection Model leaves open, and so where audits and steering should focus.

title: Three concurrent works covered parts of my plan, so I narrowed it
body: I narrowed my work to what they leave open: base models, text baselines and OLMo-2's own stages, and I re-checked Han Xiao's result on his released data.

part: 6. What they say and what I found
title: As Persona Geology predicts, the words carry most of the role
body: With the role prompt out of view, the reply words name the role about as well as the model's states do (OLMo-2-7B: 0.80 against 0.76 and 0.75).

part: 6. What they say and what I found (exploratory; agent review only)
title: In Han Xiao's data, DPO spreads all roles apart as role play doubles
body: Han Xiao reports that DPO pulls desirable roles toward the Assistant, but in his data that gap holds only in raw units, because all roles spread apart at DPO as role play doubles (Olmo 3 7B).

title: The OLMo-2-7B base model rarely plays a role from a plain description
body: I judged 3 of 20 base replies in role, against 16 of 20 for Instruct, and what the base model's states know about the role comes mostly from the prompt.

part: 7. Results: the same text read by every stage (exploratory; agent review only)
title: Every stage puts the default near the Assistant-like end, and the words alone nearly do too
body: When every stage reads the same replies, all four stages draw nearly the same role map and put the default near the Assistant-like end, as Lu et al. found, but the words alone put it there almost as well (OLMo-2-7B, 20 roles).

title: Each behaviour changes at its own stage
body: Agreeing with the user is already high at SFT, a small coin-flip lean toward the harmful task appears at DPO (exploratory), and giving in to pushback rises most at RLVR (OLMo-2-7B).

title: The Assistant's place is already in the text; the stages differ in behaviour
body: So far, the Assistant's special place in the map is already present in the text that every stage reads, while the stages differ in how the model behaves.

My hypothesis is that post-training makes the Assistant privileged mainly through what each stage writes and does, not through how it reads; my OLMo-2 own-reply run (collected, not yet analysed) can test this.
For safety, persona monitors need a text baseline, and audits should check each stage, because different risky behaviours appear at different stages.

title: Caveats
body: One OLMo-2 model size (7B), and 20 roles for the stage tests; Lu et al. used 275. The Olmo 3 7B numbers come from Han Xiao's release, not from my runs.
Every stage read Instruct-written text, not its own replies.
No link from geometry to behaviour is established yet.
These analyses had agent reviews only. No human has reviewed them, and I have not run a formal challenge of each result.

title: Next steps and questions for Thomas
body: Next, I analyse the SFT, DPO and Instruct own replies, and I rerun the position test with all 275 roles (about $25 to $120 of GPU time).
For 16 Nov: should I post the base, same-text and Han Xiao results now, with the own-reply results as a follow-up, or wait for the own-reply results?
Is a like-for-like OLMo-2 test of Han Xiao's group finding worth its cost and power?
Which meaning of "privileged" should lead: position, spread, or behaviour on the user's turn?

title: The setup and the exact prompt
body: Models: OLMo-2-7B base, SFT, DPO and Instruct (after RLVR), at pinned revisions.
20 roles from the Assistant Axis set (Lu et al. 2026), for example pirate, toddler, cynic, consultant and robot.
The default stands for the Assistant: replies with no role prompt (four identity wordings and one with no system message).
40 open questions, none of them math tasks.
Position: the default's distance from the end of the roles' main axis, on a 0 to 1 scale as in Lu et al.
Spread: how far a character's reply states sit from their own average, against the median role.
prompt:
The following is an interview. The guest answers in their own voice.

About the guest: a robot that analyzes data with mechanical precision and systematic processing methods

Interviewer: You've been struggling with a skill that seems to come naturally to others. How do you approach this?
Guest:
caption: Exact base input after one start token. The Instruct model gets its own chat template, for example system "You are a toddler who sees everything as new and exciting, asking lots of questions about the world around you.", then the user's question.

part: Backup: the coin-flip test (exploratory; my review is not finished)
title: OLMo-2-7B: a small lean toward the harmful task appears at DPO, and it depends on the prompt frame
body: Nguyen's test: the prompt offers a harmless task on one coin outcome and a harmful task on the other, then stops before the outcome. I read the next-word probabilities of "heads" and "tails".
SFT to DPO change, open user turn: -0.044 [-0.060, -0.029]. One other plain-text frame also shows a DPO lean: -0.048 [-0.085, -0.010].
My main frame drops the "Human:" start of Nguyen's template. With it kept, DPO gives -0.017 [-0.052, +0.018].
Nguyen (OLMo-3.1-32B) finds a lean toward the harmless task from DPO on. In OLMo-2-7B the change also comes at DPO, but toward the harmful task.
Limits: 20 tasks, small effects, many cells tested, and token probabilities, not the model's choices. This is not evidence that DPO installs a harmful preference.

title: The Terra judge works on chat replies and fails on base replies
caption: So judge rates on base replies, such as pod B's 15.4%, are uncertain. Base behaviour claims rest mostly on blind naming and my own reading.
